steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multi-object tracking (MOT) has been studied a lot in recent years. Its goal is to associate detected objects across video frames to get their whole moving trajectories. As tracking algorithms develop, MOT can be used in many tasks, like traffic flow analysis, human behavior prediction and pose estimation, autonomous driving assistance, and even estimating the abundance of underwater animals.

A MOT system can be divided into two main parts, the embedding model and the association algorithm. The input is multiple successive frames, and the embedding techniques and association approaches estimate the object locations and the track identities (IDs). MOT is hard because of illumination changes, occlusions, complex environments, fast camera movement, unreliable detections, and varying low image resolutions. Also, the individual steps of the tracking algorithm, such as detection, feature extraction, affinity estimation and association, can affect the tracking performance. This causes big variations and uncertainty. With recent progress in representation learning with deep neural networks, embedding methods have an essential role in estimating object locations and associating identities over time in MOT. In this survey we focus on reviewing embedding learning and not association methods, even though association methods are also important for MOT.

Embedding methods in MOT also vary a lot, just like in other computer vision tasks such as image classification, object detection, object retrieval, crowd counting, visual tracking, re-identification (Re-ID) and segmentation. But nobody has systematically analyzed and summarized the embedding learning approaches in MOT. Some embedding methods combine multi-task heads, including box regression, object classification and re-identification. Some consider spatial-temporal correlations and combine appearance and motion information. Some methods use the interaction relationships among objects with correlation and attention to learn the track embeddings. Because embedding methods differ so much, we want to do a comprehensive survey from the embedding perspective and discuss some under-investigated embedding areas and future directions.

- Existing surveys (cite)
  - Xu et al. (cite): deep learning trackers and network structures
  - Emami et al. (cite): model-based multiple hypotheses tracking with ML in detection, filtering, association
  - Ciaparrone et al. (cite): deep learning in MOT: detection, feature extraction, affinity, association
  - Park et al. (cite): evolution of MOT in recent decades, deep learning, recent advances
  - Luo et al. (cite): MOT systems from different aspects
  - ours: embedding learning, object-level representative features; analyze SOTA by embedding strategy
- Contributions
  - 1) categorize/summarize embedding methods; advantages and limitations; insights for design and new topics
  - 2) widely used benchmarks; analyze SOTA by embedding method
  - 3) under-investigated issues and future trends
- Outline
  - II related work/relevant tasks; III taxonomy and review; IV metrics and SOTA analysis; V open issues and future work; VI conclusions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multi-object tracking (MOT) has been studied a lot in recent years. Its goal is to associate detected objects across video frames to get their whole moving trajectories. As tracking algorithms develop, MOT can be used in many tasks, like traffic flow analysis, human behavior prediction and pose estimation, autonomous driving assistance, and even estimating the abundance of underwater animals.

A MOT system can be divided into two main parts, the embedding model and the association algorithm. The input is multiple successive frames, and the embedding techniques and association approaches estimate the object locations and the track identities (IDs). MOT is hard because of illumination changes, occlusions, complex environments, fast camera movement, unreliable detections, and varying low image resolutions. Also, the individual steps of the tracking algorithm, such as detection, feature extraction, affinity estimation and association, can affect the tracking performance. This causes big variations and uncertainty. With recent progress in representation learning with deep neural networks, embedding methods have an essential role in estimating object locations and associating identities over time in MOT. In this survey we focus on reviewing embedding learning and not association methods, even though association methods are also important for MOT.

Embedding methods in MOT also vary a lot, just like in other computer vision tasks such as image classification, object detection, object retrieval, crowd counting, visual tracking, re-identification (Re-ID) and segmentation. But nobody has systematically analyzed and summarized the embedding learning approaches in MOT. Some embedding methods combine multi-task heads, including box regression, object classification and re-identification. Some consider spatial-temporal correlations and combine appearance and motion information. Some methods use the interaction relationships among objects with correlation and attention to learn the track embeddings. Because embedding methods differ so much, we want to do a comprehensive survey from the embedding perspective and discuss some under-investigated embedding areas and future directions.

Some surveys of MOT have been published in recent years. Xu et al. summarize some deep learning-based trackers and deep neural network structures. Emami et al. review model-based multiple hypotheses tracking with machine learning techniques in detection, filtering and association. Ciaparrone et al. review how deep learning is used in MOT, including detection, feature extraction, affinity computation and association. Park et al. review how MOT evolved in recent decades, focusing on deep learning techniques and looking at recent advances in MOT. Luo et al. review MOT systems and discuss approaches from different aspects. Different from all these surveys, we focus on embedding learning in MOT, which means how to learn object-level representative features for the MOT task, and we analyze state-of-the-art methods in a comprehensive way based on their embedding strategies. The main contributions of the survey are:

1) We categorize and summarize the existing embedding methods for MOT and analyze them in depth and comprehensively by discussing their advantages and limitations. This gives insights for designing future algorithms and exploring new topics. 2) We summarize the widely used benchmarks and analyze the state-of-the-art approaches according to their embedding methods. 3) We discuss some important research directions with under-investigated issues related to embedding techniques and look at future trends in MOT.

The rest of the survey is organized like this. Section II shows related works, including the tasks most relevant to MOT. Section III gives a taxonomy and a detailed review of embedding methods. Section IV summarizes the evaluation metrics and analyzes the state-of-the-art approaches by embedding method. Section V discusses some under-investigated issues and points out trends and possible future studies. Section VI draws conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multi-object tracking (MOT) has been widely studied in recent years, with the aim of associating detected objects across video frames to obtain their entire moving trajectories. With the development of tracking algorithms, MOT can be applied in many tasks, such as traffic flow analysis [1,2,3,4], human behavior prediction and pose estimation [5,6,7,8], autonomous driving assistance [9,10], and even underwater animal abundance estimation [11,12,13].

The flow of MOT systems can be divided into two main parts, i.e., the embedding model and the association algorithm. With multiple successive frames as input, the object locations and track identities (IDs) are estimated via embedding techniques and association approaches. MOT is challenging due to illumination changes, occlusions, complex environments, fast camera movement, unreliable detections, and varying low image resolutions [14]. In addition, tracking performance can be affected by the individual steps of tracking algorithms, such as detection, feature extraction, affinity estimation, and association, resulting in significant variations and uncertainty. With the recent progress in representation learning with deep neural networks, embedding methods play an essential role in object location estimation and temporal identity association in MOT. In this survey, we focus on reviewing embedding learning rather than association methods [15,16,17,18], though association methods are also important in MOT.

As in other computer vision tasks [19,20,21,22], such as image classification, object detection, object retrieval, crowd counting, visual tracking, re-identification (Re-ID), and segmentation, embedding methods in MOT vary widely. However, the embedding learning approaches in MOT have never been systematically analyzed and summarized. Some embedding methods combine multi-task heads [23,24,25,26,27], including box regression, object classification, and re-identification. Some consider spatial-temporal correlations [28,29,30,31,32], combining both appearance and motion information. Others exploit the interaction relationships among objects with correlation and attention to learn track embeddings [33,34,35]. This large deviation among embedding methods motivates us to conduct a comprehensive survey from an embedding perspective and to discuss several under-investigated embedding areas and future directions.

Several surveys [36,37,38,39,40] of MOT have been published in recent years. Specifically, Xu et al. [36] summarize deep learning-based trackers and deep neural network structures. Emami et al. [37] review model-based multiple hypotheses tracking with machine learning techniques in detection, filtering, and association. Ciaparrone et al. [38] review how deep learning is adopted in MOT, including detection, feature extraction, affinity computation, and association. Park et al. [39] review the evolution of MOT over recent decades, focusing on deep learning techniques and recent advances in MOT. Luo et al. [40] review MOT systems and discuss approaches from different aspects. Unlike these existing surveys, we focus on embedding learning in MOT, i.e., how to learn object-level representative features for the MOT task, and comprehensively analyze state-of-the-art methods according to their embedding strategies. The main contributions of this survey are summarized as follows:

1) We categorize and summarize existing embedding methods designed for MOT and provide an in-depth and comprehensive analysis by discussing their advantages and limitations, which provides insights for future algorithm design and new topic exploration. 2) We summarize the widely used benchmarks and analyze state-of-the-art approaches according to their embedding methods. 3) We discuss several important research directions with under-investigated issues related to embedding techniques and take a step towards future trends in MOT.

The rest of this survey is organized as follows. We first present related works, including the tasks most relevant to MOT, in Section II. A taxonomy and detailed review of embedding methods are given in Section III. We then summarize the evaluation metrics and analyze state-of-the-art approaches according to their embedding methods in Section IV. Section V discusses several under-investigated issues and points out trends and potential future studies. Conclusions are drawn in Section VI.
